title: What you leave
hookLine: one Stoic idea that doesn't fit you

lines: ONE CHAPTER, LEFT WHERE IT IS.
cards: A friend lends you a cookbook from their grandmother's kitchen. You love it. You make the bread every Sunday now.
But there's a chapter on organ meats that you read once, out of respect, and quietly decided was not for you. You didn't throw the book away. You didn't write an angry letter to the grandmother.
You just left that chapter where it was. A year of Stoic reading can leave a chapter like that: an idea admired, or tried, or argued with, and finally set down.

teach.h: NOT OUR MASTERS, BUT OUR GUIDES.
teach.b: First, permission from Seneca himself. A committed Stoic, he still wrote that he hadn't bound himself to any one master or borne anyone's name.
The great thinkers before us, he says in another letter, are not our masters but our guides. And he quoted Epicurus, a rival, again and again, taking what was good wherever he found it.
Leaving something behind is, oddly, a very Senecan thing to do. Second, some candidates.

teach.h: SOME IDEAS ARE HARD TO LIVE WITH.
teach.b: Some readers find a few Stoic ideas hard to live with. The hope of being entirely free of passions, which can sound like numbness. The claim that health, wealth, even the people we love, are indifferent to our true good.
The old Stoic paradox that all wrongdoing is equally wrong. Epictetus's hardest words about grief. None of these is a misreading; they really are in the texts.
And serious Stoics, then and now, have argued about them too. Third, how to leave well. Not with contempt.

teach.h: NAME IT FAIRLY, THEN SET IT DOWN.
teach.b: Name the idea fairly, in its strongest form, the way the Stoics would state it. Then say plainly, without a fight: not for me. You may come back to it in ten years and find it fits.
Or not. Fourth, why it matters. Seneca read his teachers as guides, keeping some things and leaving others, and the Stoic school itself kept arguing with its founders.
Walking a philosophy as yourself is part of the tradition, not a break from it.
The porch was always open on the sides. You can step off it, and step back on.

how: Some modern readers of the Stoics adopt some of their practices while openly setting aside others, such as the ideal of being free of all passions or the paradox that all wrongs are equal.

o: the rival thinker Seneca kept quoting as a guide
a Stoic who wrote down Epictetus's lectures

games.q: not for me — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca said he had bound himself to no single master
and called earlier thinkers guides, not masters.
the hard Stoic ideas are just modern misreadings
they really are in the texts, and Stoics have argued about them too.
leaving an idea means treating it with contempt
state it fairly, in its strongest form, then set it down.

games.q: you've found a Stoic idea that doesn't fit you. what would Seneca's example suggest?
o: name it fairly and set it down, keeping the rest
games.why: Seneca called earlier thinkers guides, not masters, and borrowed from rivals; choosing is part of the path.

practice: Think back over the year for one Stoic idea that never sat right with you, and state it silently in its strongest, fairest form, the way a good Stoic would. Notice that you can understand it and still not take it on.
Then gently set it down, the way you'd close a chapter in a borrowed book: not for me, at least not now.

wordCard.voice: Epicurus, the rival philosopher Seneca kept quoting, taking what was good from any teacher, since the old thinkers are guides, not masters. Today's word.
